paragraphs.heading: Mammals with pouches
paragraphs.text: Marsupials are a varied group of mammals, the infraclass Marsupialia. Their young are born at a fairly undeveloped stage and then cared for inside a pouch on the mother's belly. Kangaroos, wallabies, koalas, wombats, opossums, possums, bandicoots and Tasmanian devils are all marsupials. The name comes from marsupium, the technical word for that pouch, which goes back through Latin to an ancient Greek word meaning "pouch".

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Marsupials are native to Australasia, Wallacea and the Americas. Of the 334 living species, close to 70% live on the Australian continent, which takes in mainland Australia, Tasmania, New Guinea and nearby islands. The rest live in the Americas, mostly in South America. Thirteen species live in Central America, and just one, the Virginia opossum, lives in North America north of Mexico.

paragraphs.heading: An old split
paragraphs.text: Marsupials and placental mammals went their separate ways 125–160 million years ago, in the Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous. Marsupials still have the usual mammal traits, such as mammary glands, three middle ear bones, true hair and bone structure. Yet clear differences, including in anatomy, set them apart. For example, they have epipubic bones that jut forward from the pubic bone of the pelvis. Because males and pouchless species have these bones too, they are thought to have first helped move the hind limbs rather than serving reproduction.

paragraphs.heading: Skulls, teeth and brains
paragraphs.text: Marsupial skulls are generally small and compact, with enlarged cheekbones that reach further back and a hard palate with more openings than in placentals. Many marsupials carry 40 to 50 teeth, a larger set than most placentals have. Early marsupials had 50 teeth, a count the opossum still keeps, while kangaroos and wallabies have fewer. Like monotremes, marsupials also lack the corpus callosum, a large connection between the right and left halves of the brain.

paragraphs.heading: A doubled system
paragraphs.text: Marsupial reproductive organs differ from those of placentals, because the reproductive tract is doubled. A female has two uteri and two vaginas, and a birth canal forms between them before birth. In most species the male has a split or double penis that sits in front of the scrotum.

paragraphs.heading: Pouches of many kinds
paragraphs.text: Most species have a pouch, but its form varies to give the young as much protection as possible. Many keep a permanent pouch, while in others, such as the shrew opossum, it develops during pregnancy and the young are hidden only by folds of skin or by the mother's fur. Kangaroos have a pouch that opens at the front, while many species that walk or climb on all fours have one that opens at the back. As a rule the pouch belongs to females, yet the male water opossum has one too, which protects his genitals as he swims or runs.

paragraphs.heading: Big and small
paragraphs.text: Marsupials have adapted to many habitats, and their bodies vary widely to match. The red kangaroo, the largest living marsupial, grows up to 1.8 metres tall and 90 kilograms in weight. The smallest, the marsupial mice, reach only 5 centimetres in body length, while extinct Diprotodon weighed several tons. Some marsupials look like placental mammals, an example of convergent evolution.
